name: David's numbering of the people
charge: Numbering Israel in pride; a plague on the nation
summary: David commanded Joab to number Israel and Judah. Joab objected; the king's word prevailed. When the count came in, David's heart smote him: I have sinned greatly. Gad offered three judgments, and David chose to fall into the hand of the Lord.
offense: The anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel, and David was moved to number the people; Chronicles names Satan as the one who stood up against Israel and provoked him (2 Samuel 24:1; 1 Chronicles 21:1). The provocation did not make David an unwilling bystander. He gave the command and pressed it against objection. Joab wished that the Lord would multiply the people a hundredfold and asked why David delighted in this thing. Chronicles records his warning that the act would bring trespass upon Israel (1 Chronicles 21:3). The king's word prevailed, and the officers went through the land (2 Samuel 24:2-8). Authority could compel the count without making the purpose acceptable. Numbering itself was not absent from the law. Exodus 30:12 required a ransom for each man when Israel was numbered, that there be no plague among them. The people were the Lord's, not a measure of strength for a ruler to possess independently of him. Joab's protest and the prescribed warning both stood against treating the census as a harmless exercise of royal pleasure. Afterward David's heart smote him. He confessed that he had sinned greatly and done very foolishly (2 Samuel 24:10). He did not place the guilt upon the officers who had obeyed him. The recognition came after the command had already carried its work through the kingdom.
judgment: Pestilence: seventy thousand men died from Dan to Beersheba in three days. The angel stood at Araunah's threshingfloor with drawn sword when the Lord said, it is enough. David bought the floor and built an altar; it became the temple site.

entries.commentary: The anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel, and he moved David to number Israel and Judah. This was the Most High wanting to judge Israel; he used David and used Satan to provoke him to do it. Joab objected, asking why the king delighted in this thing, for numbering the people was not the king's job but the work of the Levites. Notwithstanding, the king's word prevailed against Joab and the captains, and they went out to number the people. Joab did not understand that behind it all, verse one, the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel; it was of the Most High that this happened.

Joab and the captains passed over Jordan and went through all the land, from Aroer and Gad and Gilead, to Dan-jaan, to Zidon, to the stronghold of Tyre and the cities of the Hivites and Canaanites, and out to the south of Judah to Beersheba. It took them nine months and twenty days to count all of Israel. Joab gave the sum to the king: there were in Israel eight hundred thousand valiant men that drew the sword, and the men of Judah were five hundred thousand men. This did not count the women and the children.

David's heart smote him after he had numbered the people, and he said unto the Lord, I have sinned greatly; take away the iniquity of thy servant, for I have done very foolishly. As soon as it was done it hit him, because it was not the king's job but the Levites' to number the people. In the morning the word of the Lord came to the prophet Gad, David's seer, offering David three things to choose one: seven years of famine, three months fleeing before his enemies, or three days of pestilence. David was in a great strait and said, Let us fall now into the hand of the Lord, for his mercies are great, and let me not fall into the hand of man. He had two prophets, Gad and Nathan, who ministered to him.

The Lord sent the pestilence upon Israel from the morning to the time appointed, and there died seventy thousand men from Dan to Beersheba. When the angel stretched out his hand upon Jerusalem to destroy it, the Lord repented him of the evil and said to the angel, It is enough, stay now thine hand; and the angel was by the threshing place of Araunah the Jebusite. David saw the angel that smote the people, something we cannot see today, for the Most High has blinded our eyes to it and this walk is by faith and the keeping of the commandments. David spoke unto the Lord, Lo, I have sinned and done wickedly, but these sheep, what have they done; let thine hand be against me and against my father's house. Remember the reason for the seventy thousand is verse one, the Most High was angry at Israel.

Gad told David to rear an altar unto the Lord in the threshing floor of Araunah, and David went up as the Lord commanded. Araunah bowed himself before the king and offered to give the floor, the oxen, and the instruments freely for the burnt sacrifice, saying, The Lord thy God accept thee. David refused to take it for nothing, saying he would not offer burnt offerings unto the Lord his God of that which cost him nothing, and bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver. He built there an altar and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, so the Lord was entreated for the land and the plague was stayed from Israel. True worship costs us something. --- Topics: [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant) · [The Feasts of the Most High](/encyclopedia/the-feasts-of-the-most-high) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood)

Satan stood up against Israel and provoked David to number the people; David commanded Joab to number Israel from Beersheba to Dan. Joab objected, asking why the king would require this thing and be a cause of trespass to Israel, but the king's word prevailed. Joab numbered the people: a thousand thousand and a hundred thousand men that drew sword in Israel, and four hundred threescore and ten thousand in Judah. Joab left Levi and Benjamin uncounted because the king's word was abominable to him.

The Most High was displeased with the numbering and smote Israel; David confessed he had sinned greatly and done very foolishly and begged that the iniquity be taken away. The Most High sent Gad the seer to offer David three choices: three years of famine, three months of destruction before his foes, or three days of pestilence with the destroying angel. David chose to fall into the hand of the Most High rather than the hand of man, saying very great are His mercies, for he knew man would not show him the mercy the Most High would.

The Most High sent pestilence, and seventy thousand men of Israel fell; the angel was sent to destroy Jerusalem, but the Most High beheld it, repented of the evil, and told the angel it was enough to stay his hand. David lifted up his eyes and saw the angel of the Most High standing between earth and heaven with a drawn sword stretched over Jerusalem, and he and the elders, clothed in sackcloth, fell on their faces. David pleaded that he alone had sinned by commanding the numbering, asking that the hand be on him and his father's house but not on the people, who as sheep had done nothing. Our forefathers had the pleasure of seeing such acts of the Most High in their midst; in these last days we walk by faith in what the scriptures say, for the war is now of a different kind.

The angel commanded Gad to tell David to set up an altar in the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite, and David went up at the word spoken in the name of the Most High. Ornan, threshing wheat, turned and saw the angel and hid with his four sons, then saw David and bowed to the ground; David asked to buy the threshingfloor for the full price so the plague might be stayed. Ornan offered to give it all, the place, the oxen, the threshing instruments for wood, and the wheat, but David refused to take what was another man's or to offer burnt offerings without cost. David paid six hundred shekels of gold, built the altar, offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and the Most High answered him by fire from heaven and commanded the angel to sheathe his sword. David paid the full price rather than take the offering for free, and this is a pattern for Israel today: what is given to the Most High should cost the giver something. -

When David saw that the Most High answered him at the threshingfloor of Ornan, he sacrificed there. The tabernacle Moses made and the altar of burnt offering were then at the high place in Gibeon. David could not go to Gibeon to inquire of the Most High because he was afraid of the sword of the angel, so he worshipped at the new altar instead. --- Topics: [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood)

The altar to burn incense upon was made of shittim wood, a cubit in length and a cubit in breadth, foursquare, and two cubits high, with horns of the same. A cubit has been read to be about seventeen inches, so this stood about waist high. It was overlaid with pure gold, the top, the sides round about, and the horns, with a crown of gold round about, two golden rings under the crown, and staves of shittim wood overlaid with gold. The staves through the rings were how the priests bore it as Israel moved through the wilderness.

The altar was put before the vail that is by the ark of the testimony, before the mercy seat where the Most High would meet with Moses. Aaron burned sweet incense on it every morning when he dressed the lamps, and again at even when he lighted the lamps, a perpetual incense before the Lord throughout the generations; it burned continually, morning and evening. No strange incense went on it, and no burnt sacrifice, meat offering, or drink offering; this altar was for one specific incense only. The service had to be exactly as prescribed, and deviation carried death, which is a reason to thank the Lord for Christ.

Aaron made an atonement upon the horns of it once in a year with the blood of the sin offering of atonements; it is most holy unto the Lord. This altar served the day of atonement. On the tenth day of the seventh month Israel afflicted their souls and did no work at all, and the priest made an atonement for the sanctuary, the tabernacle, the altar, the priests, and all the people of the congregation, to cleanse them from all their sins before the Lord; an everlasting statute, once a year. The priests went always into the first tabernacle accomplishing the service of God, but into the second went the high priest alone once every year, not without blood. Christ offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, so the day of atonement is still kept by afflicting the soul and doing no work, but without the animal sacrifice, because Christ took the place of the animal.

Numbering the children of Israel was not done lightly; when they were counted, every man gave a ransom for his soul unto the Lord, that there be no plague among them when they were numbered. The ransom was half a shekel after the shekel of the sanctuary, from every one that passed among them that were numbered, from twenty years old and above; the rich gave no more and the poor gave no less, to make an atonement for their souls. The atonement money was appointed for the service of the tabernacle of the congregation. The gold, the wood, the curtains, and the fabrics all had to be bought and kept up, and the tabernacle moved with the nation through the wilderness; that is the same reason offerings are gathered in the congregation today, because the house of the Most High cannot be built or kept without it.

The laver of brass, with his foot also of brass, stood between the tabernacle of the congregation and the altar, with water in it; a great brass bowl set on a brass base. Aaron and his sons washed their hands and their feet thereat when they went into the tabernacle of the congregation and when they came near to the altar to minister, that they die not; the priests could not go in unclean. It was a statute for ever to Aaron and to his seed throughout their generations.

The holy anointing oil was compounded of principal spices, pure myrrh five hundred shekels, sweet cinnamon two hundred and fifty, sweet calamus two hundred and fifty, cassia five hundred after the shekel of the sanctuary, and oil olive an hin, an ointment compound after the art of the apothecary, which is a maker of perfume. With it were anointed the tabernacle of the congregation, the ark of the testimony, the table and all his vessels, the candlestick and his vessels, the altar of incense, the altar of burnt offering with all his vessels, and the laver and his foot, that they be most holy; whatsoever toucheth them shall be holy. Aaron and his sons were anointed and consecrated with it to minister in the priest's office. It was not poured upon man's flesh, and none was to be made like it after the composition of it; whosoever compounded any like it, or put any of it upon a stranger, was cut off from his people. The Most High gave specific orders down to the spices and the weights, and none could deviate from them or they would die. Our forefathers carried out that tedious, exact work, yet we complain about the smallest things set in place for order, the uniform, the new moon, and not cooking on the sabbath; the spirit has to get right.

The perfume was made of sweet spices, stacte, onycha, and galbanum, with pure frankincense, of each a like weight, tempered together, pure and holy, a confection after the art of the apothecary. Part of it was beaten very small and put before the testimony in the tabernacle of the congregation; unto you it shall be most holy. The Most High wanted the tabernacle anointed and smelling sweet, everything done one specific way. It was for the Lord alone; ye shall not make to yourselves according to the composition thereof, and whosoever made like unto it, to smell thereto, was cut off from his people. There were no knockoffs of the holy things; a copy carried death.

Hashabiah the son of Kemuel: of the Aaronites, Zadok: 18 Of Judah, Elihu, one of the brethren of David: of Issachar, Omri the son of Michael: 19 Of Zebulun, Ishmaiah the son of Obadiah: of Naphtali, Jerimoth the son of Azriel: 20 Of the children of Ephraim, Hoshea the son of Azaziah: of the half tribe of Manasseh, Joel the son of Pedaiah: 21 Of the half tribe of Manasseh in Gilead, Iddo the son of Zechariah: of Benjamin, Jaasiel the son of Abner: 22 Of Dan, Azareel the son of Jeroham. These were the princes of the tribes of Israel. 23 But David took not the number of them from twenty years old and under: because the LORD had said he would increase Israel like to the stars of the heavens. 24 Joab the son of Zeruiah began to number, but he finished not, because there fell wrath for it against Israel; neither was the number put in the account of the chronicles of king David. 25 And over the king’s treasures was Azmaveth the son of Adiel: and over the storehouses in the fields, in the cities, and in the villages, and in the castles, was Jehonathan the son of Uzziah: 26 And over them that did the work of the field for tillage of the ground was Ezri the son of Chelub: 27 And over the vineyards was Shimei the Ramathite: over the increase of the vineyards for the wine cellars was Zabdi the Shiphmite: 28 And over the olive trees and the sycomore trees that were in the low plains was Baal-hanan the Gederite: and over the cellars of oil was Joash: 29 And over the herds that fed in Sharon was Shitrai the Sharonite: and over the herds that were in the valleys was Shaphat the son of Adlai: 30 Over the camels also was Obil the Ishmaelite: and over the asses was Jehdeiah the Meronothite: 31 And over the flocks was Jaziz the Hagerite. All these were the rulers of the substance which was king David’s. 32 Also Jonathan David’s uncle was a counsellor, a wise man, and a scribe: and Jehiel the son of Hachmoni was with the king’s sons: 33 And Ahithophel was the king’s counsellor: and Hushai the Archite was the king’s companion: 34 And after Ahithophel was Jehoiada the son of Benaiah, and Abiathar: and the general of the king’s army was Joab.*

verses.text: And again the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel, and he moved David against them to say, Go, number Israel and Judah.

For the king said to Joab the captain of the host, which was with him, Go now through all the tribes of Israel, from Dan even to Beer–sheba, and number ye the people, that I may know the number of the people.

And Joab said unto the king, Now the Lord thy God add unto the people, how many soever they be, an hundredfold, and that the eyes of my lord the king may see it: but why doth my lord the king delight in this thing?

Notwithstanding the king’s word prevailed against Joab, and against the captains of the host. And Joab and the captains of the host went out from the presence of the king, to number the people of Israel.

And David’s heart smote him after that he had numbered the people. And David said unto the Lord, I have sinned greatly in that I have done: and now, I beseech thee, O Lord, take away the iniquity of thy servant; for I have done very foolishly.
For when David was up in the morning, the word of the Lord came unto the prophet Gad, David’s seer, saying,
Go and say unto David, Thus saith the Lord, I offer thee three things; choose thee one of them, that I may do it unto thee.

So Gad came to David, and told him, and said unto him, Shall seven years of famine come unto thee in thy land? or wilt thou flee three months before thine enemies, while they pursue thee? or that there be three days’ pestilence in thy land? now advise, and see what answer I shall return to him that sent me.
And David said unto Gad, I am in a great strait: let us fall now into the hand of the Lord; for his mercies are great: and let me not fall into the hand of man.
So the Lord sent a pestilence upon Israel from the morning even to the time appointed: and there died of the people from Dan even to Beer–sheba seventy thousand men.

And David spake unto the Lord when he saw the angel that smote the people, and said, Lo, I have sinned, and I have done wickedly: but these sheep, what have they done? let thine hand, I pray thee, be against me, and against my father’s house.
And Satan stood up against Israel, and provoked David to number Israel.
And David said to Joab and to the rulers of the people, Go, number Israel from Beer–sheba even to Dan; and bring the number of them to me, that I may know it.

And Joab answered, The Lord make his people an hundred times so many more as they be: but, my lord the king, are they not all my lord’s servants? why then doth my lord require this thing? why will he be a cause of trespass to Israel?
Nevertheless the king’s word prevailed against Joab. Wherefore Joab departed, and went throughout all Israel, and came to Jerusalem.

And Joab gave the sum of the number of the people unto David. And all they of Israel were a thousand thousand and an hundred thousand men that drew sword: and Judah was four hundred threescore and ten thousand men that drew sword.
But Levi and Benjamin counted he not among them: for the king’s word was abominable to Joab.
And God was displeased with this thing; therefore he smote Israel.
And David said unto God, I have sinned greatly, because I have done this thing: but now, I beseech thee, do away the iniquity of thy servant; for I have done very foolishly.
So the Lord sent pestilence upon Israel: and there fell of Israel seventy thousand men.

And God sent an angel unto Jerusalem to destroy it: and as he was destroying, the Lord beheld, and he repented him of the evil, and said to the angel that destroyed, It is enough, stay now thine hand. And the angel of the Lord stood by the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite.

And David lifted up his eyes, and saw the angel of the Lord stand between the earth and the heaven, having a drawn sword in his hand stretched out over Jerusalem. Then David and the elders of Israel, who were clothed in sackcloth, fell upon their faces.

And David said unto God, Is it not I that commanded the people to be numbered? even I it is that have sinned and done evil indeed; but as for these sheep, what have they done? let thine hand, I pray thee, O Lord my God, be on me, and on my father’s house; but not on thy people, that they should be plagued.
And king David said to Ornan, Nay; but I will verily buy it for the full price: for I will not take that which is thine for the Lord, nor offer burnt offerings without cost.
So David gave to Ornan for the place six hundred shekels of gold by weight.
And David built there an altar unto the Lord, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and called upon the Lord; and he answered him from heaven by fire upon the altar of burnt offering.

When thou takest the sum of the children of Israel after their number, then shall they give every man a ransom for his soul unto the Lord, when thou numberest them; that there be no plague among them, when thou numberest them.
But David took not the number of them from twenty years old and under: because the Lord had said he would increase Israel like to the stars of the heavens.
Joab the son of Zeruiah began to number, but he finished not, because there fell wrath for it against Israel; neither was the number put in the account of the chronicles of king David.

lawsResolved.text: Pride and arrogance brings decline, punishment and destruction.
You are not to trust in the abundance of your riches, for he who trusts in his riches will fall.
Punishment is given by disease and pestilence.
